summary: Meta and Binghamton authors describe a three-agent pipeline (bill-of-materials domain classifier, failure-mode extractor, test-case author) that turns hardware self-healing validation documents and bills of materials into structured fault-injection test plans for two production AI-datacenter rack platforms. The plans add 23 and 19 generated cases to 31 and 37 extracted spec entries, reported as '+74.2% / +51.4% coverage'. A three-Claude judge panel passes 75-83% of the additions, and one engineer per platform accepts 18/23 and 13/19. This is hardware validation, not software development; the generator model, prompts and data are proprietary.

claims.claim: Coverage expansions of 74.2% and 51.4% over manually authored baselines
claims.evidence: Table IV: test-case counts 31 -> 54 and 37 -> 56. The 'baseline' is the framework's own extraction of the input document, so the increase is non-negative by construction, and no failure-mode or component coverage metric is computed. Counting only human-accepted additions gives +58% and +35%.
Fig. 4: judged only by the three Claude reviewers (31/31, 37/37 in all replications); human annotators reviewed only generated entries.

claims.claim: Authoring burden reduced from days to hours
claims.evidence: No timing, effort or cost measurement appears anywhere in the body; the claim is asserted in the abstract and §V-A prose.

claims.claim: High expert acceptance of new scenarios, and the LLM judge panel is calibrated to experts
claims.evidence: Table VI: 18/23 (78.3%) and 13/19 (68.4%) accepted. §IV-C promises two annotators and inter-annotator agreement, but §V-B reports one engineer per platform and no agreement figure. Calibration is inferred only from aggregate rates falling inside the judge range; no item-level human-LLM agreement is given.

claims.claim: Fully traceable mapping from each test case to its source specification
claims.evidence: §III-C5: each case carries a provenance tag (from spec vs agent-generated); link correctness is never verified or measured.

patterns.note: A per-item provenance tag (source spec vs generated) is called 'full traceability'; it is a label, not a verified link, and link accuracy is not measured.
A platform-specific domain enumeration and sample part descriptions per sub-category constrain the classifier; not compared with an unconstrained run.

Three-Claude majority-vote panel run 3 times (per-model SD up to 10.2 pp; Sonnet 4.6 passes 94.7% vs Opus 4.5 71.9% on Platform B). Aggregate pass rates bracket the single human rater's, but no item-level agreement is reported.
Three-agent decomposition with parallel classifier and extractor; no single-agent or single-prompt comparison.
Framed as a human-in-the-loop draft; engineers rejected 11/42 additions (redundant, unsafe to inject, physically untestable).
Production inputs from two real platforms, but no field outcome: generated tests are not reported as executed and no defects found are reported.

methodology.sample: 2 production platforms; 68 extracted spec entries; 42 generated test cases (23 + 19)
methodology.baselines: The input specification's own entries; no manually authored plan from the same inputs, no single-agent or prompt-only baseline
methodology.models: Generator LLM undisclosed (hosted in-house); judges Claude Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.5
methodology.variance: Judge panel replicated 3 times (mean +/- SD); generator run once per platform

standards.artifacts: None; internal orchestration tools, models and data are proprietary (§III-D)

biases.detail: 'Coverage' is a count of test cases, not coverage of failure modes or components; about a quarter of the added cases are rejected by humans.
The baseline is the pipeline's own input, so any addition counts as expansion.
Extraction fidelity is judged by LLMs only; judge calibration is argued from aggregate rates, not item-level agreement.
42 generated items, one human rater per platform, generator run once.
Generator model, prompts, inputs and outputs unavailable.
Meta authors evaluate a Meta-internal tool with Meta engineers as raters.
No tokens, runtime or engineer-hours reported, despite the 'days to hours' claim.
Table VII: 'All rejections are scope decisions, not quality failures', yet one rejection is a physically untestable case and two are unsafe injections.

coi.affiliations: Meta Platforms (3 authors, including the corresponding author); Binghamton University (3 authors)
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Meta-internal agentic tooling (not a sold product); Anthropic models used only as judges
coi.detail: Company team evaluating its own internal tool on its own platforms with its own engineers; no independent replication.

verdict_reason: Off-topic for this KB: hardware fault-injection test planning, not software development with agents. Its headline numbers also rest on test-case counts against its own input, an unmeasured time saving and a single human rater per platform.
applicability: Does not transfer as evidence. A loose analogy: converting domain source documents into schema-conforming structured records with a per-item provenance tag resembles content ingestion. The rejection taxonomy (redundant with existing coverage, needs institutional or safety knowledge) is a reminder that generated artifacts still need someone with domain knowledge to filter them, which is exactly what new developers lack.
